title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Minaya's vow; the spoils sold to the Moors; the march to Alcocer (tiradas 24–26, lines 493–556)
part: Tiradas 24–26 · Minaya's vow; the spoils sold to the Moors; the march to Alcocer (lines 493–556)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 158–162, lines 493–556 (tiradas 24–26). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t: —“Mucho vos lo gradesco, Campeador contado.
sentences.l: —“Much to-you it I-thank, Campeador renowned.
sentences.i: —“I thank you greatly for it, renowned Campeador.
sentences.n: Tirada 24 (assonance á-o) — Minaya will take no share of the spoils and makes a solemn vow. The endings run contado, mandado, Castellano, quitado, alto, cavallo, campo, malo: stressed á, then o. Minaya answers the Çid's offer of the fifth (v. 492). gradesco = agradezco, 'I thank'. contado, 'renowned' (literally 'counted, reckoned'), the Campeador's standing epithet. The dash and quotation mark are Pidal's, opening Minaya's speech, which runs to v. 505.

sentences.t:
D’aquest[e] quint[o] que me avedes mand[ad]o,
pagar se ya dell[e] Alfonsso el Castellano.
sentences.l:
Of this fifth that to-me you-have ordered,
be-satisfied himself would with-it Alfonsso the Castilian.
sentences.i: With this fifth you have assigned me, Alfonso the Castilian himself would be content.
sentences.n: aquest[e] quint[o], mand[ad]o, dell[e]: the bracketed letters are Pidal's restorations (his italics); aqueste = este, delle = dél, 'of it' (de + él with the old final -e). el quinto or la quinta is the fifth part of the booty (Pidal's note to v. 515; the Çid offered it as la quinta, v. 492). pagar se ya = se pagaría, 'would be satisfied': the split conditional, the infinitive and the ending -ya (= -ía) held apart by the pronoun se, as buscar nos ie at v. 528. pagarse is 'to be pleased, content' (cf. pagado, v. 412). Even a king would be pleased with such a share: the praise makes the refusal larger.

sentences.t: Yo vos l[o] suelt[o] e avello quitado.
sentences.l: I to-you it release and have-it remitted.
sentences.i: I release it back to you, and hold it given up.
sentences.n: l[o] suelt[o], again with Pidal's restored final vowels. soltar 'to release, let go'; quitar here is 'to remit, quit a claim' (of a debt or right). avello is aver + lo, the r of the infinitive taken into the l (averlo > avello); how the line is built is not certain: most simply, 'and (I declare that I) have it remitted', i.e. the renunciation is done and binding. The legal pair suelto … quitado gives the refusal the sound of a formal waiver.

sentences.t:
A Dios lo prometo, a aquel que está en alto:
fata que yo me pague sobre mio buen cavallo,
lidiando con moros en el campo,
que enpleye la lança e al espada meta mano,
sentences.l:
To God it I-promise, to that-one who is on high:
until that I myself be-satisfied upon my good horse,
fighting with Moors in the field,
that I-employ the lance and to-the sword I-put hand,
sentences.i: To God I promise it, to Him who is on high: until I have had my fill upon my good horse, fighting the Moors in the open field, plying the lance and setting hand to the sword,
sentences.n: The vow. a aquel que está en alto echoes the Çid's own prayer at v. 8 (que estás en alto). fata que = hasta que, 'until' (f- for modern h-). me pague, present subjunctive of pagarse: Minaya plays on the word of v. 495: the king would be satisfied with the fifth; Minaya will be satisfied only by fighting. lidiar, 'to fight'. v. 499 is short (Pidal prints it as he has it). enpleye = emplee, subjunctive of enplear, 'use, put to work'. al espada: before a vowel the old feminine article is el, so a + el espada > al espada, 'to the sword'; meter mano a, 'set hand to'.

sentences.t:
e por el cobdo ayuso la sangre destellando,
ante R[o]y Díaz el lidiador contado,
non prendré de vos quanto un dinero malo.
sentences.l:
and by the elbow down the blood dripping,
before Roy Díaz the fighter renowned,
not I-will-take from you as-much-as one penny bad.
sentences.i: with the blood trickling down past my elbow, before the eyes of Ruy Díaz, the renowned fighter, I will not take from you so much as one wretched penny.
sentences.n: por el cobdo ayuso, 'down along the elbow': cobdo = codo; ayuso = 'down' (Latin deorsum). destellar, 'to drip, trickle'. The arm streaming with blood to the elbow is the poem's picture of a man who has fought with his whole body; the line returns as a formula later in the poem (Pidal's note sends the reader to his introduction). R[o]y: only the o is Pidal's (Roy = Ruy, Rodrigo). prendré, future of prender, 'take'. un dinero malo: the dinero was the smallest coin; malo, 'bad, debased', so 'not one miserable penny'. Minaya's speech goes on to v. 505, where the quotation mark closes.

sentences.t:
Pues que por mí ganaredes quesquier que sea dalgo,
todo lo otro afelo en vuestra mano.”
sentences.l:
Since that through me you-shall-win whatsoever that be of-something,
all the other behold-it in your hand.”
sentences.i: When through me you have won something of real worth, then I will take it; till then, all the rest — see, I leave it in your hands.”
sentences.n: Pidal glosses: 'after you have won through me anything that is good, I will take it; but until then, all the rest I leave in your hands' — an ellipsis: the clause 'then I will take a share' is left unspoken. Pues que, 'after, once'. ganaredes, 2nd pl. of the courteous vos: Pidal's paraphrase has the future ganaréis; the same letters also spell the future subjunctive (ganáredes), which a clause of future time often takes, so the tense is not certain. quesquier = cualquier cosa, 'whatever'. dalgo = de algo, 'of something', i.e. of worth (as in fija dalgo). afelo = afé + lo, 'behold it, here it is' (the presentative fe/afé, as fellos v. 485): he hands it all back.

sentences.t: Estas ganançias allí eran juntadas.
sentences.l: These gains there were gathered.
sentences.i: These spoils were gathered together there.
sentences.n: Tirada 25 (assonance á-a) — the Çid sells his fifth to the Moors, and will not fight King Alfonso. The endings: juntadas, espada, compañas, mesnadas, falla, carta, plata, presentaja, agua, Minaya — stressed á, then a. ganançias here are the spoils of Castejón and of Minaya's raid.

sentences.t:
Comidiós mio Çid, el que en buen[a çinxo espada],
[e]l rey Alfonsso que llegarién sus compañas,
quel buscarie mal con todas sus mesnadas.
sentences.l:
Bethought-himself my Çid, the-one who in good (hour) [girded sword],
[th]e king Alfonsso that would-arrive his companies,
that-him would-seek harm with all his households.
sentences.i: My Çid, who girded on his sword in a good hour, bethought himself that King Alfonso's companies would come, and that he would seek to do him harm with all his men.
sentences.n: Comidiós = comidió + se, 'reflected, realized' (Pidal: 'se dio cuenta, reparó, pensó'). The formula el que en buena çinxo espada, 'he who girded on his sword in a good hour', with its close [a çinxo espada] restored by Pidal; buena agrees with an understood ora, 'hour'. [e]l, Pidal's letter. el rey Alfonsso, the subject of the clause, is drawn ahead of the que that introduces it: 'that King Alfonso — his companies would come'. llegarién, buscarie: conditional in -ién/-ie (= llegarían, buscaría). quel = que le, 'that (he) … him': the enclitic squeeze. compañas and mesnadas, the king's troops and households.

sentences.t:
Mandó partir tod aqueste aver [sin falla],
sos quiñoneros que gelos diessen por carta.
sentences.l:
He-ordered to-divide all this wealth [without fail],
his share-men that them-to-them should-give by writing.
sentences.i: He ordered all this wealth to be divided, without fail, and his share-masters to give them their portions in writing.
sentences.n: tod aqueste aver: tod(o) cut before a vowel; aver is the noun 'wealth' (v. 484). [sin falla], 'without fail', a stock filler of the á-a assonance, here Pidal's restoration. The quiñoneros were the officers who divided the booty into quiñones, shares. gelos = ge (= les, 'to them') + los: Pidal notes the loose construction: los refers to the quiñones, a noun not stated but contained in the word quiñoneros. por carta, 'by document': each man's share set down in writing.

sentences.t:
Sos cavalleros i an arribança,
a cada uno dellos ca[d]en çient marcos de plata,
e a los peones la meatad sin falla;
todo [el] quint[o] a mio Çid fincava.
sentences.l:
His knights there have good-fortune,
to each one of-them fall a-hundred marks of silver,
and to the foot-soldiers the half without fail;
all [the] fifth to my Çid remained.
sentences.i: His knights did well there: to each of them fell a hundred marks of silver, and to the foot-soldiers half as much, without fail; the whole fifth remained to my Çid.
sentences.n: arribança: Pidal reads 'good fortune, a prosperous state', and rejects the usual rendering 'were admitted to the sharing' (the knights were in any case first in the share-out). i = 'there'. ca[d]en = caen, 'fall (to)', with Pidal's restored older -d- (Latin cadere). A marco was a mark-weight of silver. peones, 'men on foot'; meatad = mitad, 'half'. [el] quint[o], Pidal's letters; fincar, 'to remain'. The tenses wander, present an, caden, imperfect fincava: epic tense-mixing.

sentences.t:
Aquí non lo puede vender nin dar en presentaja;
nin cativos nin cativas non quiso traer en su conpaña.
sentences.l:
Here not it he-can sell nor give in present;
nor captive-men nor captive-women not he-would bring in his company.
sentences.i: Here he could neither sell it nor make a gift of it; and he would not take captives, men or women, along in his company.
sentences.n: presentaja, 'present, gift' (Pidal); at v. 522 the same word will mean an offer of price. Aquí, in this place, Castejón; the poem does not say why, but the next lines have him sell the fifth to the neighbouring Moors instead. nin … nin … non: the double negative, the closing non not cancelling but strengthening. cativos, cativas, 'captives', the Moors taken at Castejón (see vv. 534–541).

sentences.t:
Fabló con los de Castejón, y envió a Fita y a Guadalfajara
esta quinta por quanto serié conprada,
aun de lo que diessen oviessen grand ganançia.
sentences.l:
He-spoke with those of Castejón, and sent to Fita and to Guadalfajara
this fifth for how-much would-be bought,
even of what they-should-give they-should-have great gain.
sentences.i: He spoke with the people of Castejón, and sent to Hita and to Guadalajara to ask what price this fifth would fetch — and even at what they gave, they would have made a great bargain.
sentences.n: Fita and Guadalfajara are most likely Hita and Guadalajara (as at v. 446), Moorish towns of the Henares country through which Minaya raided (vv. 446, 480); Fita keeps the f- that modern Spanish turns to h-. y here is 'and' (usually e). The sense is compressed: he sent to them (to ask) for how much this fifth would be bought (conprada, the past participle agreeing with quinta); serié = sería. Pidal glosses v. 520 'aunque de lo que diesen tuviesen gran ganancia', i.e. 'even though they offered very little': by his reckoning the fifth was worth more than 11,000 marks, against the 3,000 paid (v. 521). aun = aunque; oviessen, imperfect subjunctive of aver, 'have'.

sentences.t:
Asmaron los moros tres mill marcos de plata.
Plogo a mio Çid d’aquesta presentaja.
sentences.l:
Reckoned the Moors three thousand marks of silver.
It-pleased to my Çid of this offer.
sentences.i: The Moors set the price at three thousand marks of silver. My Çid was pleased with the offer.
sentences.n: Asmaron, from asmar, 'to reckon, estimate' (Latin aestimare). Plogo, strong preterite of plazer, 'it pleased' (= plugo). presentaja, now 'an offer, a price proposed' (Pidal's note to this line), not 'gift' as at v. 516.

sentences.t: A tercer dia dados f[o]ron sin falla.
sentences.l: At third day given were without fail.
sentences.i: On the third day the marks were paid, without fail.
sentences.n: dados f[o]ron = fueron dados, 'they were given', i.e. the 3,000 marks were paid; the past participle first, the auxiliary after it. f[o]ron: Pidal's older o (as f[o]sse, v. 61). A tercer dia, 'on the third day'. sin falla again fills out the á-a.

sentences.t:
Asmó mio Çid con toda su conpaña
que en el castiello non i avrie morada,
e que serie retenedor, mas non i avrie agua.
sentences.l:
Reckoned my Çid with all his company
that in the castle not there would-be dwelling,
and that it-would-be holdable, but not there would-be water.
sentences.i: My Çid and all his company considered that there would be no staying in the castle: it could be held, but there would be no water there.
sentences.n: Asmó: the same asmar, now 'considered, judged'. i = 'there'. avrie = habría (non i avrie, 'there would not be', impersonal aver as modern hay). morada, 'a dwelling, a stay'. retenedor, 'holdable, defensible', a rare form: a place that could be retained against assault. A fortress without water cannot stand a siege; the Çid's next camp will be chosen for its water (v. 555).

sentences.t:
“Moros en paz, ca escripta es la carta,
buscar nos ie el rey Alfonsso, con toda su[e] mesnada.
Quitar quiero Castejón, oid, escuelas e Minaya!
sentences.l:
“Moors in peace, for written is the charter,
seek us would the king Alfonsso, with all his household.
To-leave I-want Castejón, hear, troops and Minaya!
sentences.i: “The Moors here are at peace with the king, for the charter of it is written; King Alfonso would come after us with all his household. I mean to leave Castejón — hear me, my men, and Minaya!
sentences.n: The Çid speaks; the speech runs on across the tirada break and closes at v. 538. Moros en paz, ca escripta es la carta: Pidal explains it from the Tercera Crónica General, 'King Alfonso has peace with the Moors, and I know the charters of it are already written': these Moors were under Alfonso VI's protection, and the king punished Christians who attacked such subject Moors. ca, 'for'. buscar nos ie = nos buscaría, 'would seek us': the split conditional with the pronoun inside. su[e], the old possessive sue with Pidal's restored -e. quitar, 'to leave, quit'. oid = oíd, 'hear'. escuelas, 'troops, household men' (Pidal: = mesnadas).

sentences.i: Do not take amiss what I am going to say: we could not stay on in Castejón; King Alfonso is close, and he will come looking for us.
sentences.n: Tirada 26 (assonance á) — the Çid marches into the lands of Zaragoza, dependent on the Moorish king of Valencia (Pidal's rubric). The endings carry a single stressed á: mal, fincar, verná, hermar, plaz, están, adelant, Taranz, Bivar, grand; words with a weak -e after the á count with them (parten, v. 540; plaz, adelant and grand are the forms with that -e cut). The new assonance comes in the middle of the Çid's speech. dixier[o], future subjunctive of dezir, 'shall say', with Pidal's -o. non lo tengades a mal, 'do not hold it as ill'; tengades = tengáis. podriemos = podríamos. fincar, 'to stay'. çerca es: ser for place, where modern Spanish has está. buscar nos verná = vendrá a buscarnos: verná is the future of venir without the d; the infinitive hangs on a verb of motion without a.

sentences.i: Yet I do not want to leave the castle empty: a hundred Moorish men and a hundred Moorish women I mean to set free here, so that they shall not speak ill of me for having taken it from them.
sentences.n: hermar = yermar, 'to leave waste, unpeopled' (yermo, 'desert'). el castiello non lo, çiento moros … las: the object stated first, then taken up by a pronoun. quitar is here 'to set free' (Pidal); [i], 'there', is his restoration. Pidal takes it that the Çid frees only these two hundred, cedes the castle to them, and gives or sells them the rest of the captives; the Crónica Particular del Cid understood it much the same way. por que … que: the que is said twice around the inserted clause lo pris dellos; the link is loose: most likely 'so that they may not speak ill of me for having taken it from them'. pris, 1st sing. strong preterite of prender, 'took'.

sentences.t:
Todos sodes pagados e ninguno por pagar.
Cras a la mañana pensemos de cavalgar,
con Alfons mio señor non querría lidiar.”
sentences.l:
All you-are paid and none for to-pay.
Tomorrow in the morning let-us-set-about to-ride,
with Alfons my lord not I-would-wish to-fight.”
sentences.i: You are all paid, and no one is left unpaid. Tomorrow morning let us take to our horses; with Alfonso, my lord, I would not wish to fight.”
sentences.n: sodes = sois. ninguno por pagar, 'none (is left) to be paid'. Cras, 'tomorrow' (Latin cras; modern mañana); a la mañana, 'in the morning'. pensemos de cavalgar: pensar de + infinitive, 'set about'. Alfons, a short form of the name, not at the rhyme (as del rey Alfons, v. 33). querría, conditional of querer. The exile still calls the king who banished him mio señor: the Çid is a vassal who will not fight his lord, the poem's constant thread. The speech closes here.

sentences.i: What the Çid had said pleased all the others. From the castle they had taken they all depart rich, and the Moorish men and women stand blessing him.
sentences.n: plaz = plaze (place), 'pleases', cut short for the á. prisieron, strong preterite of prender, 'took'. se parten, 'depart'. bendiziéndol están = le están bendiciendo, 'are blessing him': gerund with the enclitic l(e), estar + gerund. The freed Moors bless the man who took their castle: the poem's ideal of a lord generous even to the conquered.

sentences.t:
Vansse Fenares arriba quanto pueden andar,
troçen las Alcarrias e ivan adelant,
sentences.l:
Go-off-themselves Fenares up as-much-as they-can travel,
they-cross the Alcarrias and were-going forward,
sentences.i: They go off up the Henares as fast as they can travel; they pass through the Alcarrias and pressed on ahead,
sentences.n: Vansse = van + se, 'they go off'. Fenares = Henares (f- for h-), the river, arriba, 'upstream'. quanto pueden andar, 'as much as they can go'. troçen, from troçir, 'to pass through'. The Alcarrias (Pidal: from Arabic qarya, 'village') are the uplands that make up most of the modern province of Guadalajara. Present, imperfect (ivan), preterite (v. 545) all in one sentence: tense-mixing again. adelant = adelante, cut for the á.

sentences.t:
por las Cuevas d’Anquita ellos passando van,
passaron las aguas, entraron al campo de T[a]ranz,
por essas tierras ayuso quanto pueden andar.
sentences.l:
through the Caves of Anquita they passing go,
they-crossed the waters, they-entered into-the plain of T[a]ranz,
through those lands down as-much-as they-can travel.
sentences.i: they go on by the Caves of Anquita, crossed the waters, came out onto the plain of Taranz, and go on down through those lands as fast as they can travel.
sentences.n: Anquita is Anguita, on the river Tajuña east of Sigüenza (Pidal); he says nothing of the Cuevas. passando van, ir + gerund, 'go passing'. passaron las aguas: which waters is not said; perhaps the Tajuña, perhaps the divide of waters that Pidal's note on Taranz describes. The Campo de T[a]ranz (the a is Pidal's) is part of the high plateau dividing the waters of the Tajuña and the Jalón, on the border of the provinces of Guadalajara and Soria. por essas tierras ayuso, 'down through those lands', now down toward the Jalón.

sentences.t: Entre Fariza e Çetina mio Çid iva albergar.
sentences.l: Between Fariza and Çetina my Çid went to-lodge.
sentences.i: Between Ariza and Cetina my Çid went to lodge for the night.
sentences.n: Pidal identifies Fariza and Çetina as Ariza and Cetina, on the Jalón, in the province of Zaragoza; why the poem's form has F- is not clear. iva albergar, ir + infinitive as a plain past ('went to lodge' = 'lodged'), as iva posar (v. 402).

sentences.t:
Grandes ganançias priso por la tierra do va;
non lo saben los moros el ardiment que an.
sentences.l:
Great gains he-took through the land where he-goes;
not it know the Moors, the daring that they-have.
sentences.i: He took great spoils through the land he passes through; the Moors do not know the bold designs his men have in mind.
sentences.n: priso, strong preterite of prender. do = 'where' (= donde). non lo saben … el ardiment: lo anticipates the object stated after it. ardiment, 'daring, a bold design' (cut for the á). Pidal glosses: 'the Moors do not know the designs of the Çid's men', so the subject of an (= han, 'have') is the Çid's company; the line is compressed and the reading not certain.

sentences.t:
Otro día moviós mio Çid el de Bivar,
e passó a Alfama, la Foz ayuso va,
passó a Bovierca e a Teca que es adelant,
sentences.l:
Next day moved-himself my Çid the-one of Bivar,
and passed to Alfama, the Gorge down goes,
passed to Bovierca and to Teca that is ahead,
sentences.i: Next day my Çid, he of Vivar, broke camp, passed by Alhama and went on down the gorge; he passed Bubierca, and Ateca that lies beyond,
sentences.n: Otro día, 'the next day'. moviós = movió + se, 'set out'. el de Bivar, 'he of Vivar', an epithet from his home. Alfama is Alhama, on the Jalón 6 km from Cetina (Pidal); la Foz, 'the gorge' (hoz): Pidal says only that it will be a gorge of the river, now unpeopled, so the spot is not certain. Bovierca and Teca: Pidal's Bubierca and Ateca, on the Jalón, 5 and 11 km from Alhama; in a Teca the a may be both preposition and the town's first letter. es adelant, 'is further on'.

sentences.i: and my Çid went to camp over against Alcocer, on a round hill, strong and high; close by runs the Jalón, so no one can cut him off from water.
sentences.n: sobre Alcoçer, 'over, against Alcoçer': to camp sobre a town is to sit down before it, threatening a siege. Alcoçer is now unknown; Pidal places it to the left of the Jalón, between Ateca and Calatayud. otero, 'hill, knoll'; grand cut for the á. Salón is the river Jalón. agua nol puedent vedar: vedar agua is to cut off a besieged enemy's water (Pidal), the very lack that ruled out Castejón (v. 526). nol = no le; puedent = pueden, the old -nt of the plural kept in the spelling; the subject, the Moors, is understood.

sentences.t: Mio Çid don Rodrigo Alcoçer cueda ganar.
sentences.l: My Çid don Rodrigo Alcoçer thinks to-win.
sentences.i: My Çid, Don Rodrigo, means to win Alcocer.
sentences.n: cueda = cuida, from cuidar, 'to think, intend', not yet modern 'take care'. ganar, 'to win, take'. The line points ahead: with the host camped on the hill (vv. 553–555), the next tirada turns to the taking of Alcoçer.
